title: Christians do not say that God has a body
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος διὰ πλειόνων τὰ μὴ λεγόμενα ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν τιθεὶς ὡς λεγόμενα ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὡς σώματος τῇ φύσει τυγχάνοντος καὶ ἀνθρωποειδοῦς σώματος, ἀνατρέπειν ἐθέλει τὰ μὴ τεθειμένα ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν, ἅπερ περισσὸν παραθέσθαι ἢ τὴν ἀνατροπὴν αὐτῶν. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἃ λέγει ἡμᾶς φάσκειν περὶ θεοῦ ἐλέγομεν, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἵστατο, ἀναγκαῖον ην ἡμῖν τὸ τιθέναι τὰς λέξεις αὐτοῦ καὶ κατασκευάζειν μὲν τὰ ἡμέτερα λύειν δὲ τὰ ἐκείνου· εἰ δ᾿ ἑαυτῷ συνείρει ἃ ἤτοι ἀπ᾿ οὐδενὸς ἤκουσεν ἢ, ἵνα καὶ δοθῇ ὅτι ἤκουσεν, ἀπό τινων ἁπλῶν καὶ ἀκεραίων καὶ μὴ εἰδότων τὸ τοῦ λόγου βούλημα, οὐ χρὴ ἡμᾶς τευτάζειν περὶ τὰ μὴ ἀναγκαῖα. σαφῶς γὰρ ἀσώματόν φασιν οἱ λόγοι τὸν θεόν· διὸ καὶ „θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε πώποτε,“ καὶ „εἰκὼν“ λέγεται εἶναι „τοῦ ἀοράτου θεοῦ ὁ πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως,“ ὡς εἰ ἔλεγεν ἀσωμάτου. μετρίως δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων καὶ περὶ θεοῦ διειλήφαμεν ἐξετάζοντες, πῶς νοοῦμεν τὸ „πνεῦμα ὁ θεὸς, καὶ τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτὸν ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν.“
pass_a_gloss: Next after these, Celsus, through more words (διὰ πλειόνων) setting down (τίθημι) things not said by us as said by us about God, as being (τυγχάνω) a body (σῶμα) by nature (φύσις) and a human-formed (ἀνθρωποειδής) body, wishes to overturn (ἀνατρέπω) things not laid down by us, which it is superfluous (περισσός) to quote (παρατίθημι) or their overturning (ἀνατροπή). For if we were saying what he says we assert (φάσκω) about God, and he were standing (ἵστημι) against them, it would be necessary for us to set down his words (λέξεις) and to establish (κατασκευάζω) ours and to undo/refute (λύω) his; but if he strings together (συνείρω) for himself things which he heard either from no one, or, that it may also be granted (δίδωμι) that he heard, from some simple (ἁπλοῖ) and guileless (ἀκέραιοι) people not knowing the intent (βούλημα) of the word/teaching (λόγος), we need not busy ourselves (τευτάζω) about things not necessary. For clearly the words/Scriptures (οἱ λόγοι) say God is incorporeal (ἀσώματος); wherefore also 'no one has ever (πώποτε) seen (ὁράω) God,' and 'image (εἰκών)' is said to be 'of the invisible (ἀόρατος) God the firstborn (πρωτότοκος) of all creation (κτίσις),' as if it said 'of the incorporeal.' Moderately (μετρίως) in the things before these we have discussed (διαλαμβάνω) also about God, examining (ἐξετάζω) how we understand (νοέω) 'God is spirit (πνεῦμα), and those worshipping (προσκυνέω) him must worship in spirit and truth (ἀλήθεια).'
pass_b_english: After this, Celsus at some length sets down, as if they were said by us, things about God that we do not say: as though God were by nature a body, and a body of human form. And he wishes to overturn positions we have not laid down, which it is superfluous to quote, or his refutation of them either. For if we said what he claims we assert about God, and he were taking his stand against that, we would have had to set down his words, to establish our own position and to undo his. But if he strings together for himself things that he either heard from no one, or, granting even that he heard them, heard from some simple and guileless people who do not know the intent of our teaching, we need not busy ourselves with what is not necessary.

For our Scriptures plainly say that God is incorporeal. That is why “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), and “the firstborn of all creation” is said to be “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), as if it said “of the incorporeal God.” We have also dealt with God adequately in what came before, when we examined how we understand “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

choices.choice: Celsus’s long argument against a God with a human-shaped body is not quoted by Origen, so there is no Celsus quotation in this chapter. τὸ τοῦ λόγου βούλημα is rendered ‘the intent of our teaching’ and οἱ λόγοι ‘our Scriptures’; both refer to the Christian word as set out in Scripture. The claim that the Scriptures ‘plainly’ call God incorporeal is Origen’s; the word ἀσώματος itself is not biblical, and Origen draws it from the texts he then quotes. Colossians 1:15 is quoted with the order rearranged (εἰκὼν ... τοῦ ἀοράτου θεοῦ, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως). μετρίως (‘in measure, adequately’) is rendered ‘adequately’. ‘What came before’ refers back to Origen’s discussion of John 4:24 earlier in the work (notably 6.70–71); the cross-reference was not re-checked against those chapters. ‘Spirit’ in John 4:24 is lower-cased in ‘God is spirit’ and ‘in spirit and truth’, since it names God’s nature and the manner of worship, not the Holy Spirit.
No change to the English: negations (things not said, not laid down), the counterfactual 'we would have had to', and the concessive 'granting even that he heard them' all match the Greek

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
